issues.legal_issue: An immovable-property sale made without payment or a promise of future payment does not transfer ownership.
material_facts: The deeds purported to transfer parts of jointly owned immovable property to the seller’s wife and minor sons and recorded that consideration had been paid.
No evidence established that the wife or sons had paid the stated consideration or had the means to do so.
The courts below found that the seller had not proved payment of the consideration, and that finding was not disturbed.
issues.conclusion: The deeds were void for want of consideration and transferred no title. The appellant retained an undivided half share and was entitled to joint possession.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a sale is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price, which may be paid, promised, or partly paid and partly promised. Payment of price is essential; where an immovable-property sale is made without payment and the deed makes no provision for payment in the future, it is not a sale in law and has no effect. The Court relied on no earlier cases.

predicates.civil_property_title_proceeding: The parties litigated a civil dispute over title to immovable property.
predicates.immovable_property_sale: A document purported to transfer ownership of immovable property by sale.
predicates.consideration_not_paid_or_promised: The alleged price was not paid, and the transaction made no provision for payment of the price in the future.

issues.definition: When a civil property-title dispute concerns an immovable-property sale for which no price was paid or promised, the sale is void and transfers no title.

issues.legal_issue: A party need not seek a declaration to challenge a void document, and a limitation objection to an unnecessary declaratory claim does not arise.
material_facts: The original pleadings sought relief based on the appellant’s asserted joint ownership and specifically alleged that the deeds were void because they were without consideration.
The deeds were found void for want of consideration.
The claims for declarations concerning the deeds were added by amendment after the suits had begun.
issues.conclusion: A separate declaration invalidating the deeds was not necessary because their invalidity had been pleaded and could be established in the proceedings. The limitation issue concerning the added declaratory prayers therefore did not arise.
issues.legal_principle: A void document need not be challenged by a claim for declaration; its invalidity may be pleaded and proved even in collateral proceedings. Since a declaration was unnecessary on the facts, the Court did not need to decide whether the amended declaratory prayers were time-barred. The Court relied on no earlier cases.

predicates.civil_property_title_proceeding: The parties litigated a civil claim concerning rights in immovable property.
predicates.void_document: The document relied on to assert a transfer of rights was established to be void.
predicates.underlying_title_asserted: The claimant sought relief on the basis of an asserted title independent of the void document.

issues.definition: In a civil property-title proceeding, when the relied-on document is void and the claimant asserts underlying title, a separate declaration invalidating the document is not required.
